en: The Scripture of the One-Syllable Uṣṇīṣa-Cakra King Spoken at the Place of Enlightenment,
Fascicle One.
[By] the Grand Master of the Court, of Equal Rank with the Three Dukes, Special Advancement, Acting Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial.

Translated by the Tripiṭaka Śramaṇa Amoghavajra of Daxingshan Monastery—Grand Master of the Three Great Wisdoms, conferred the purple robe and the title of Minister of Works, posthumously honored as the Great Mirror, Duke of Sū State with a fief of three thousand households, and bearing the posthumous name Dajian—by Imperial Decree. Because the mantra practices of great bodhisattvas such as Avalokiteśvara are made manifest;

"O Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, we pray that you will speak upon the essential points of the Dharma verses of the *Naya*.

Performing great Buddha-activities in all worlds;
the most supreme phrase among all samādhis.

In this land of great merit,

The perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, and so forth;

and the radiance emanating from the marks of a Great Man.

In this way, from every locus of the vidyā-mantras of all Tathāgatas,
light is emitted;
within each individual ray of light, immeasurable rays of light serve as its retinue.
From the crown of the Buddha’s head, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of light rays issued forth—
of various colors such as blue, yellow, red, white, and purple—
illuminating immeasurable buddha-fields.
Illuminating all the hells and the animal realms of this trichiliocosm,

establishing all mantra practices.
It brings about all meaningful benefits for all bodhisattvas,
accomplishes the adornment of great merit,
and easily achieves all forms of peace and happiness.
In a single instant, having accomplished all meaningful benefits,
he causes the palaces of Māra in Buddha-worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges to wither and fade away.
It eclipses all the light of Māra,
extending from the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra) down to the Avīci Great Hell,
reaching every limit and location.
Radiating brilliant light that awakened all sentient beings,
they then circled the World-Honored One three times to the right and each dissolved back into their respective original locations.
Chapter Two: Manifesting the Great Majestic Power of Mantras. From the *Ekākṣara-uṣṇīṣa-cakra-rāja-sūtra* Spoken at the Site of Enlightenment. At that time, the Tathāgata Śākyamuni...

listen now attentively to the Great Vidya-Queen of the Single-Syllable Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa, as well as the four great Buddha-uṣṇīṣas, the ūrṇā-kośa, and so forth."

the upholding of the Great Mantra.

Then one should enter the water, reaching up to the waist or the chest, [to ward off] the obstacles of the Vināyakas and the various evil creatures within the water.

By recollecting this, all those who dwell in the waters and would wish to cause harm shall have their mouths bound;
thus protecting this land, divide the land into three parts.
Use this for washing: from the feet up to the knees, rub the thighs with earth until they are clean.
Freeing them from foul odors and impurities—this the Buddhas declare to be purity. Next, use the second portion.
From the waist up to the neck—this is the third part to be washed;
one should wash the upper portion with earth.
Having removed insects, one may then place the third portion of earth and wash again with great care.
Using the *karmakara-mantra*, the practitioner consecrates water by reciting it three times and sprinkles it upon their crown.
Having bathed in tranquility and silence until they are completely purified, they must not speak with anyone.
Furthermore, by means of the *Kṛtyānuṣṭhāna* Vidyā, the practitioner performs self-consecration with the *Ajita* protection;
and by means of the *Uṣṇīṣavijayā* Vidyā,
which destroys [obstacles] with the Buddha’s *ūrṇā-kośa*, they provide universal protection and praise.
Using the Buddha-Eye mantra, which is exclusively for use within the Buddha Family,
one should bind the boundaries of the cardinal directions and intermediate points for the accomplishment of the maṇḍala, as well as protect the companions.
It is permitted to use [this] for destroying [obstacles], accomplishing all [aims],
and sprinkling insect-free water. This clarifying mantra, recited once, is as follows:
This is the mantra for ablution, used universally in the Tathāgata family.
Immediately proceeding to the recitation chamber,
one should abide in meditative concentration without negligence and visualize a space measuring three feet before one’s body.
Endowed with a mind of compassion and accompanied by wisdom,
one should proceed to the recitation chamber; there, one should wear pure garments,
such as those made of *nūpura*, *kṛmija* (silk), or wild hempen cloth.
The wise practitioner should recite [the mantra] according to the ritual procedures;
they should recite the purification mantra. Next, using the vidyā for accomplishing activities, they should consecrate a seat of kusha grass and spread it before the image.
One should recite the mantra of the *iṣṭadevatā*; next, one should invite the assembly of noble beings with the corresponding mantras and mudrās.
Visualizing the form of the *iṣṭadevatā* for a set number of times, one should then form the lotus mudrā and offer it as a seat.
The Buddhas uphold auspiciousness; from the marks upon the Buddha’s feet arise the lotus seats of all Bodhisattvas.
These seats are praised by those who practice mantras; one should not sit upon high beds.
One should then visualize the image of the Honored One. Next, one should hold the rosary and recite the mantra for stringing the beads:
"With a rosary made of bodhi seeds, one will certainly attain accomplishment."
For the superior, middling, and inferior siddhis, one should use gold, silver, and so forth for beads when employing various mantras;
for the rite of increase (puṣṭi), use pure crystal;
and for the accomplishment of all aims (sarvārthasādhaka).
The thread for the youth should be strung according to the complete ritual procedures;
one should employ one's own secret mantra to perform the consecration.
The mantra for consecrating the beads is as follows:
One should empower the rosary with this mantra and recite it seven times;
holding it in both palms while seated upon a mat of *kuśa* grass,
one should seek the accomplishment of all aims.
The auspicious *śrī-vajravṛkṣa*, white sandalwood, celestial wood (*devadāru*),
and other such species of trees— beads made from these should be used for increasing [attainments],
for superior recitation, and during *homa* rituals.
The khadira wood tree— using this wood for beads in the *mudrā* of *kuṇapa*,
one performs the rite of subjugation;
likewise, one uses this same tree wood to construct a bed and seat.
If one cannot obtain wood, one may take leaves free from insects to sit upon or lie upon;
at the site of consecration, one should sit upon them and burn the ashes of *gomaya* (cow dung);
having filtered water, one should use it for purification.
Use fine silk to make a water-strainer; carefully inspect and filter the water, and maintain the secret mantras according to the ritual rules.
If success is not attained, one should employ the Uṣṇīṣacakravartin;
through his empowerment, success will surely be achieved.
Furthermore, apply the mind and follow the mind, chanting together in harmony.
If it is not accomplished in this way, chant while harmonizing with the Buddha-eye mantra.
This is the World-Honored One’s Buddha-eye vidyā.
That which has been spoken by all Buddhas, And praised by the Buddhas of the past, I now proclaim.
Those who seek the crown of Buddhahood should recite and uphold it; Recite it in harmony with them.
One will quickly achieve accomplishment; even if one has committed the five deeds of immediate retribution, one shall likewise achieve it before long.
If there is no painted image, one may practice meditative contemplation by directing the mind; this is praised by all Buddhas.
Then, joining the palms in the gesture of salutation to the Buddha, one contemplates the practice and recites this vidyā-mantra:
*Namo ratnatrayāya alavile svāhā*. Thereupon, one binds the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*).
Visualize upon that seal a mountain composed of immeasurable jewels; atop the mountain,
visualize a lotus flower composed of the seven precious gems.
Its flowers have immeasurable thousands of millions of petals;
its calyx is vast and its stalk broad.
Above that is a multi-storied pavilion.
Within the pavilion, one should visualize the World-Honored One seated,
with a body like that of a mantra-deity,
as described in the painted image.
The World-Honored One is at ease,
sitting in the full lotus posture and forming the mudrā of preaching the Dharma.
He was endowed with the marks of a great man,
his body was adorned with them,
and he was surrounded by a pervasive, circular halo of light.
One should contemplate in this manner.
The others are also as depicted in the image above,
visualized as being within the multi-storied pavilion.
On the upper part of the pavilion is a *cakra* (wheel) finial;
one should visualize within it an immeasurable net of genuine jewels covering everything,
even extending as far as one desires to observe, up to the size of a *yojana*.
One should practice the contemplation of [the body] as being one hundred yojanas, up to even a thousand yojanas in measure;
contemplating it according to one's own inclination,
one should focus the mind with single-minded concentration all the way to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).
The wise should not be negligent;
with their minds focused on the empowering power of the tutelary deity and the Buddhas,
they should reflect as follows.
The seeker of accomplishment performs the following visualization practice.
To empower the mantra of the great ocean with the Mantra of the Stainless Ocean, one recites:
Oṃ vimalanāde hūṃ. To empower the mantra of the mountains with the Mantra of the Mountains, one recites: [Oṃ parvate hūṃ].
Oṃ āḥ jvaḥ hūṃ. The mantra for consecrating the lotus with the Lotus Mantra is:
Oṃ hūṃ kamala svāhā. The mantra for consecrating the pavilion with the Universal Jewel Pavilion Mantra is: [Oṃ sarvaratnakūṭāgāra svāhā].
*Namo sarvatathāgatebhyas tadyathā khaṃ vairocanate sphara imaṃ gaganakaṃ svāhā.* Next, one should invite the Buddha, the World-Honored One.
Using one's own mantra,
one should visualize the Blessed One descending from the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven to Jambudvīpa and proceeding to the site of enlightenment;
then, offering arghya water, one should recite this verse:
Abiding by means of one's own supernormal powers, one awaits the performance of offerings;
thereafter, one binds the boundary of the upper direction with the six-syllable Buddha-uṣṇīṣa mantra.

Then, one visualizes the Tathāgata’s bathing, as well as one's own tutelary deity (iṣṭadevatā), the lords of the three families (trikula), or those according to one's own tradition and various other deities.
One should offer incense, flowers, clothing, ornaments, food and drink, and perfumed water.
If one lacks the aforementioned offerings,
one should offer them by means of mental visualization.

Having thus completed the ritual of offering, one should then perform the confession of transgressions, rejoicing in merit, the exhortation [to the Buddhas], the dedication of merit, and the making of vows; all of these should be practiced.
Then, settle the mind upon the tip of the nose.
Recite with single-minded devotion until you are weary,
offering the prescribed number of recitations.
Furthermore, present offerings of unguents, flowers, incense, food and drink, lamps, and so forth.
Having offered argha and visualized the World-Honored One being escorted out through the eastern gate,
one should pay homage to all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas;
having paid homage, one rises.
These three times should be performed;
this ritual manual is taught for the sake of those who lack [physical] images.

Chapter Six: Distinguishing the Secret Signs. From the *Ekākṣara-uṣṇīṣa-cakra-varti-rāja-sūtra* Spoken at the Place of Enlightenment, Chapter Six: Distinguishing the Secret Signs. At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha...
Again, he addressed the Lord of Secrets, Vajrapāṇi, saying:
"Listen, Vajrapāṇi!
This is the practice for the accomplishment of the mantra of this King of Uṣṇīṣas."
This was spoken by all the Tathāgatas for the sake of accomplishing the Buddha-uṣṇīṣa;
it is taught through the practice of indestructible verses.
Vajrapāṇi briefly explains the sequence of accomplishments taught by all the Tathāgatas,
and speaks these verses:
"Gather the noble assembly in a secluded place, a location where spiritual power may be attained."
In a house or a celestial chamber, in an empty dwelling or a cave,
beneath a solitary tree or in a cemetery, or in a forest or mountain valley—
having accomplished [the practice], one should perform the recitation with the mind fixed upon the tutelary deity.
That which is impure is purified; that which is impure is thoroughly purified within purity.
By means of these two, the two are accomplished;
such a one is called an achiever (*sādhaka*), who accomplishes all *siddhis* through cultivation.
One should observe moderation in eating—neither overeating nor starving; one's intake of food and drink should be balanced.
One should abandon such craving for sweet, sour, and acidic flavors, as well as for sentient beings who are possessed by craving.
One develops craving and attachment for flavors; due to thoughts of craving, one does not perform *homa* with a single-minded focus.
One should recite the authentic scriptures during the first watch of the night and sleep during the middle watch upon a clean mat of *kuśa* grass.
Performing the protection according to the ritual manual, one should remain in union with the mudrās;
reclining like a lion, as brave and courageous as a lion,
one sleeps with the head toward the east or the south, resting the head upon the hand.
The breath increases during the homa;
if one is facing southeast, place the left hand upon the right. The feet are likewise;
having stacked the feet, one should then lie down, making them slightly dignified.
If the head is directed toward the west, one should face the south;
when sleeping, one should protect the body in accordance with the rite of subjugation.
If ascending a white sandalwood tree or a *nyagrodha* tree of auspiciousness, [one should likewise maintain this posture].
The udumbara tree and others— dreaming of ascending such trees is a sign of accomplishment.
Geese, kalaviṅkas, ruddy sheldrakes,
white cranes, peacocks, and other auspicious birds.
If one dreams of riding upon such birds, or if one sees such signs, accomplishment (*siddhi*) shall soon be attained.
If one sees blood in a dream, this too is a sign of accomplishment. If one sees [this] within a dream...
When banners and streamers are intermingled, or when one ascends a high tower,
walks upon it, or wanders there— these are signs of accomplishment.
Or if in a dream one rides in a boat, or holds a *kīṃśuka* lute or a *vīṇā* harp.
Or seeing a stūpa, a bhikṣu, and so forth—
such auspicious dreams are all signs of accomplishment. If, within a dream, one sees a dog,
a caṇḍāla, leeches, or oil smeared upon the body.
All of these are inauspicious; if one sees or touches camels, donkeys, chariots, and the like, accomplishment will surely be ruined.
Such are the characteristics of dreams, whether they be auspicious or inauspicious signs.
One should understand these two dreams; having understood them, one should perform the homa rite to seek accomplishment.
By burning non-glutinous rice and sesame seeds, one will be liberated from all demonic obstacles and shall immediately behold the deity.
He is constantly able to provide awakening; the Noble One speaks these words:
"One should go to such-and-such a place; upon arriving there and burning ghee and honey, the actual reality will manifest.
Go and eat it until it is exhausted—this is the truth."
This is also true regarding the path. If you have doubts about the deity, you should go to sleep and wait for a dream;
there, may the Honored One manifest my body as a male form.
If you see a woman, [it is not the deity].
One should not give rise to a mind of lustful attachment;
one should practice heedfulness when about to sleep.
While reciting mantras, one should not think of past wealth and treasures, nor should one think of the future.
Be careful not to give rise to discursive thoughts;
if the ritual of recitation is not accomplished, and the mind becomes distracted, one should contemplate the meaning of the mantra and recite while dwelling in meditative concentration.
If the mind should become attached to desire, [one must restrain it].
One should practice the contemplation of impurity;
if anger arises in the mind, one should immediately apply it to loving-kindness.
If thoughts repeatedly arise regarding the conditions of ignorance, they exist within perversion.
Then, with single-minded concentration, abide in the visualization of the deity.
If you have not entered the maṇḍala circle, you must offer incense, flowers,
and so forth as food for the various māras, because [otherwise] one does not rely upon the ritual procedures.
Furthermore, for those who do not extensively and skillfully understand [the teachings], and who distance themselves from the ācārya,
various māras will follow them like shadows following forms;
their merit from recitation will be snatched away by the mere scent of the māras' food and so forth.
Through recitation and *homa*, the tutelary deity (*iṣṭadevatā*) will accept [the offering];
this sovereign of mantras shall be accomplished.
One should employ the *Uṣṇīṣa-mantra* for empowerment, as well as for the practice of *rakṣā* (protection) and *uṣṇīṣa-kriyā* (crown-rites), and so forth.
It cannot be obstructed; thus, for the sake of accomplishing the Cakravartin, one should perform the empowerment.
At all places of accomplishment, one should recite the Aparājita mantra and perform the self-consecration.
The Bodhisattva Seed Mantra: using the retinue of the Wheel-Turning King to perform protection;
when accomplishing the mantra through recitation, homa, and so forth, one should first perform the rite of self-protection.
If one departs from the methods for protecting the body, siddhi will certainly not be attained;
because the great yakṣas who roam the sky and the accomplished ghosts and rākṣasas wander about to cause destruction,
they will cause the mind to fall into doubt.
Flowers of the *vilva* tree, *arka*, *dhattūra*,
and all such [others] should not be used at all; for the *Uṣṇīṣa* section of all Buddhas,
one praises *jāti* flowers, blue lotuses (*utpala*), and *kunduru*.
The *padma-yukti* (the lotus-arrangement), as well as various other flowers of extreme fragrance and terrestrial blossoms—
one should know that by making offerings at all times with these *uṣṇīṣa-mantras*,
the practitioner will not fail to achieve success.
Perform the ritual two or three times, up to seven times in succession to achieve accomplishment.
One should perform the *mudrā-stūpa* rite at a river that flows into the ocean,
doing so once, twice, thrice, four times, or five times.
Perform these according to one's capacity:
recite mantras, construct stūpas, and offer respectful praise;
when weary from repeatedly reading and reciting the sublime scriptures, complete three hundred thousand stūpas.
All prior sins will be completely extinguished by using the most exquisite flowers,
incense, and unguents to make offerings at each and every stūpa, empowering them with mantras.
For each and every stūpa, one should recite the mantra one thousand and eight times.
If success is not achieved because the mind is obscured by transgressions,
one should construct one thousand stūpas, each measuring one cubit in size.
Even if one has committed the five deeds of immediate retribution, one will certainly achieve accomplishment;
by reciting [the mantra], one's sins are extinguished—
how much more so for one who constructs a *caitya* at a river that flows into the ocean and offers one hundred thousand lotuses?
If one offers as many as you have counted, one will swiftly attain accomplishment;
even when entering the rivers and seas, how much more so if one exceeds this measure?
Whether accomplishment is attained quickly or slowly depends entirely upon one's own person.
One who accomplishes the mantra will, through that merit—
or rather, the lack thereof— quickly attain *siddhi* in no long time if their merit is powerful; however, for one who lacks merit...
One should construct a stūpa; because the essence of *siddhi* lies in recitation, one should achieve firm accomplishment through diligence.
A mantra found in written scriptures cannot eliminate the various poisons.
Seeing such principles, one should diligently apply oneself to recitation;

it is superior to constantly serving as a parent or teacher. One should perform recitation for even a single portion of those sentient beings who undergo suffering, dedicating the merit for their sake entirely.
To extinguish all obstacles and difficulties, one should constantly pay homage to the Buddha.
Through the recitation performed while paying homage to the Buddha, one swiftly attains accomplishment.
It is said that the fruit of paying homage to the Buddha is an immeasurable mass of merit.
Know that this is the refuge; by repeatedly and diligently prostrating with reverence, one will constantly attain siddhi.
Otherwise, in the age of the Dharma’s decay, mantras will not be accomplished. Therefore, I, Śākyamuni—
It is said that these disciples of majestic power shall attain liberation in the final age;
therefore, free from doubt, they should exert great diligence and practice all *siddhis*, and before long they will achieve accomplishment.
Those who increase their superior merit will swiftly attain siddhi;
For those with little merit, it is achieved only after a long delay.
If compassion and wisdom are in union, one attains the most excellent siddhi.
Not with artificial lapis lazuli, nor with red crystal;
this is the Buddha-uṣṇīṣa mantra, whose power and function are inconceivable.
Having requested food and purified it, one should offer it to the *iṣṭadevatā*.
Divide [the portion] into three parts: out of compassion for sentient beings, one should first take one part;
it should be offered to the primary deity, and another part should be given to guests who have come from outside.
The remaining one portion should be eaten by oneself;
the food offered to the *iṣṭadevatā* should be redeemed and consumed.
If there are no guests, give it instead to birds and beasts; this is the portion for oneself.
One should not give away everything, for fear of harming the body;
one should give only a small portion. One should eat facing south;
this is the method of self-discipline. One should not eat facing west.
One should perform the rites of subjugation; for pacifying, increasing, and accomplishing, the [directions] are north-east and so forth.
For the peaceful [rite], the east is different;
one should act with a mind of compassion and contemplate [the deity] during the three times of day.
Whoever is in suffering, I now deliver them all,
endowed with a heart of great compassion; whether they be renunciants or householders,
staff-bearers or brahmins— toward all, I harbor a mind of pity and mercy.
The practitioner who wanders alone, always remaining vigilant,
therefore constantly pays homage to the stupas and shrines of all Buddhas,
reciting mantras that are difficult to accomplish while remaining in meditative equipoise at all times.
One who constantly cultivates samādhi and attains mastery over various means of subduing others should manifest various forms; therefore,
one should always perform recitation and homa.
Having smeared, wiped, and sprinkled for purification, one should perform the ritual of purification as previously explained;
thereafter, one should perform the protection of the body.
Using ashes and mustard seeds, one should bind the cardinal directions with the *kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-mantra*, or else use the *Vajrapātāla* (Cruel Topknot) mantra.
Having empowered the thread and wound it around the stakes, one should drive them into the four corners;
having thus performed the protection, one should make offerings.
Then the wise practitioner should invoke all the noble assemblies at the site of recitation and homa.
One should place [the deity] upon the seat;
as a cause for accomplishment, one should mix it with cow dung.
The wise person should construct a maṇḍala, and within this maṇḍala-circle, the ritual of offering is taught.
First, for the Victorious Tathāgata, one should offer according to the ritual manual;
next, to the Uṣṇīṣas of the Wheel-Turning Kings;
thereafter, to the Uṣṇīṣas of all Buddhas, making offerings in successive order; and finally, to Avalokiteśvara.
One's own clan together with its retinue, as well as that offered to Vajrapāṇi, is the same as for the Uṣṇīṣas;
the incense, flowers, and so forth offered are likewise according to their respective families. Thus, these constitute the three families.
And perform the ritual of offering;
by this, one should constantly remain alert toward all worldly devas. Fools speak these words:
"All practitioners of mantras are entirely acting falsely."
If one does not recite the ritual manual, one falls into slander;
yet by performing homa with sesame and white mustard seeds, one can accomplish the rite of subjugation.
One should burn sesame and non-glutinous rice.
Having obtained the *vṛddhi* [consecration], perform *homa* with poison and *rohiṇī* mixed together;
all those who disrupt and destroy the Buddha’s teaching shall be utterly extinguished. [Use] the *vilva* tree wood.
Aśoka and śveta-arka, palāśa, bodhi, and śrīparṇī—
using such woods as these for the performance of homa rites that increase prosperity; also nyagrodha and udumbara.
The wood of the aśvattha tree, the wood of the son-sustainer (putrañjīva) and others—
if one performs a rite for pacifying calamities, one should use these as fuel for the homa:
khadira wood, vibhītaka, and kālānusāri wood.
Kāravīra wood— and other such woods—
for the purpose of subjugating those who harbor mutual hatred: one should sit facing south,
reciting the syllable *HŪṂ* while burning them, performing the rite with mental intent while reciting it aloud.
One should perform the rite of subduing;
facing north, by adding *svāhā* to the mantra syllables and reciting it, pacification (*śānti*) is accomplished.
One should practice this for all the Buddha-uṣṇīṣas.
Sitting facing east, perform the *homa* for increase; sit in the *paryaṅka* (lotus) posture for pacification.
Sit in the *śrī-āsana* (auspicious) posture for increase, and in the *utkuṭaka* (crouching) posture for subjugation.
Perform the *homa* for the purpose of averting harm.
It is called the "Activity of Subjugation" because it obstructs all hindrances;
it is called "Pacification" because it brings about the fulfillment of one's wishes;
and this is called "Augmentation," as it is so in all such instances.
One should practice with careful reflection;
because it causes those who harbor malice toward the Buddha’s teachings to distance themselves, this is called the "Dharma of Mutual Hatred.
For one who maintains the pure recitation, long nails and hair should not be kept.
For a lay practitioner of pure conduct, long hair is not a transgression;
however, when performing *homa* and recitation, it creates all manner of obstacles.
The effort spent on grooming and bathing is wasted, as time passes in vain.
When making offerings to the noble assembly, one may have filth and grime in one's nails,
hair growing with lice, and the capacity to generate various transgressions;
one should not observe the time of sunrise, nor observe the time of a solar eclipse.
One should not observe a lunar eclipse;
one should not look on while making offerings to the Sangha or honoring one's teachers;
nor should one observe matters of pleasure or engage in watching quarrels. Therefore, the practitioner—
Always remaining in union with meditative concentration,
one should not seek siddhi in a land of famine, in a place of war,
where the sovereign is discordant, or where the noble assembly is being punished.
In places where yakṣas and spirits dwell, in places where nāgas and deities are intermingled,
in foul and defiled charnel grounds, in the abodes of mlecchas,
in places swarming with mosquitoes and gadflies, or in regions of severe drought.
Just as in those various places of difficulty— places where one should not seek accomplishment,
such as the quarters of unbridled prostitutes or regions with many harsh winds—
in such locations, one shall not attain *siddhi*.
In this place, if it is auspicious, the assembly of noble ones will all rejoice in the recitation and the performance of homa;
just as a person’s mind finds satisfaction upon eating fine food, so too is the homa performed herein supreme.
To accomplish all activities: if a king lacks the requisite marks, he is unfit to succeed to the throne;
likewise, inferior practitioners should perform recitation and homa according to their respective capacities.
The karmic retribution will likewise be inferior. If one begs for poison, weapons, or staffs, one should not grant them;

however, this excludes the practice of *anurāgaṇa* (the rite of attraction) and cases where it is for the sake of protecting one's life from danger or for the purpose of removing sorrow and affliction.
Except for such causes and conditions, one should never give [the vessel] to those who practice pure conduct;
if it is accidentally touched by the impure,
one should bathe and recite mantras while forming mudrās in the mind.
In this way, those classes of beings defiled by greed—
whether they be malevolent spirits, vetālas, or yakṣas— should contemplate the pure mantra, recite the vidyā, and perform mudrās; thus, all shall attain purification from their impurities.
And the accomplishment of the rākṣasas; in these superior and middling ritual sites, the wise should harbor no doubt.
Having plunged into the sublime river and bathed in the waters of the True Dharma, they contemplate with wisdom.
One should perform all recitations while maintaining the full lotus posture;
one must not break it, for doing so contradicts the requirements of the rite.
If the full lotus posture is broken, one should immediately rise and bathe, or else perform a mental bath.

Furthermore, for the benefit [of others], this accomplishment of the activity is taught.

if one possesses the ritual procedures, it will certainly be accomplished regardless of the time or planetary positions,
and without regard for the place of recitation.
One should invoke the deity to seek all siddhis and to summon others;
or, having taken the six parts,
one should perform empowerment in this manner and explain the characteristics of recitation.
When the time for the *nāva* [mantra] arrives, if the protective dharmas are lacking,
there will be spirits who steal the vital essence of humans,
as well as *ḍākinīs* and others who plunder the articles of accomplishment and steal inconceivable treasures.
At the time of recitation, everything will undoubtedly be lost;
one who has reached the end of their own life through the supreme *saṃvara* that cannot be destroyed shall sever the *maṣa*.

place the right hand palm-down over the left hand,

like a kingdom without a sovereign, or like a forest without green grass.

like a brahmin without the Vedas, like a fire sacrifice without clarified butter,

With the left hand, as before, form the *nakha-mudrā* (nail-seal);
extend the arm toward the body.

The Buddha-tooth Great Majestic Virtue Seal is conjoined with its mantra.

Oṃ tathāgata-antaḥre hūṃ phaṭ svāhā. This follows the previous armor mudrā.

bend the arms and let the fists hang downward.

All undertakings are accomplished by means of binding this mudrā;

Always forming such mudrās, one obtains great power;
regarding that Buddha-enlightenment, one always receives the prediction of attainment.

"Because of the accomplishment of great majesty, evil persons cannot obstruct or destroy it;

Possessing mindfulness and great diligence, in all places of birth,
firmly maintain the restraint of the precepts (*śīla*). As before, form the armor mudrā (*kavaca-mudrā*),
slightly contracting the index fingers.

this is the Tathāgata’s Arm Seal (*bhuja-mudrā*), which possesses great power.

*Namo samantabuddhānāṃ* *puṅ-gi-li-puk*. With the right hand, press the thumb upon the nails of the middle, ring, and little fingers.

Namo samantabuddhānām kaṭa (the syllable *kaṭa* is pronounced with a short vowel).

extend the middle and index fingers straight upward.

*Namo samantabuddhānām oṃ prasiddhikari svāhā.* Then, using the previously described eye-mudrā, slightly bend the middle and ring fingers.

Namaḥ samantabuddhānām oṃ jvalini svāhā. With the thumb of the right hand...

keep the remaining three fingers upright and slightly bent.

*Namo samantabuddhānām oṃ hūṃ hūṃ ma ma phaṭ svāhā*. Perform the light-flame mudrā as previously described.

the little and ring fingers are as before.

One should practice this; each should abide by their own discipline and properly maintain it.
Furthermore, he addressed Vajrapāṇi:
As it is said: "The practitioner who cultivates the mantra of the Buddha-uṣṇīṣa has already attained an accomplished body,
like the sun's orb first rising."
With necklaces of pure gold and armlets,
they possess the color of Jāmbūnada gold;
all manner of ornaments adorn their bodies.
Clad in exquisite celestial garments and endowed with all the marks and signs of excellence,
his body was perfectly proportioned in height and breadth, his physical form extraordinary,
and adorned with hundreds of thousands of rays of light.
His halo extends one fathom, surpassing the orb of the sun and outshining all physical forms.
Furthermore, Vajrapāṇi:
He is an accomplished vidyādhara;
merely seeing him brings joy to all sentient beings,
just as a wish-fulfilling tree satisfies every aspiration.
Furthermore, Vajrapāṇi, having accomplished the Buddha-uṣṇīṣa Cakravartin Bodhisattva,
rains down various kinds of sublime celestial food and drink upon the hells,
and is likewise able to fulfill all that sentient beings require.
All those who have hopes shall have them fully satisfied.
I have briefly described that he possesses great majesty and power.
This is the mantra for the accomplishment of the Vajrapāṇi Cakravartin.
They fulfill the aspirations of all sentient beings;
by merely forming a thought in their minds, they bring them to fulfillment.
Such are those who have attained the accomplishment of a Wheel-Turning King.
Bodhisattvas dwelling on the ten stages do not dare to transgress its instructions and commands.
O Vajrapāṇi, this is the mantra of the Sovereign of the Single Syllable Wheel.
The king among all mantras,
the sovereign of great vidyā-kings;
if one practices this, all karmic obstacles will be extinguished.
Furthermore, it eradicates all karma leading to the evil realms.
Upon accomplishing this mantra,
all supernatural powers will manifest before one.
In the mere twinkling of an eye, he went to the Akaniṣṭha heaven,
where all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Śrāvakas praised him with joy;
there he attained all the practices of the Bodhisattvas.
They travel with sovereign mastery through other worlds,
according to the inclinations of all sentient beings.
They preach the Dharma through various sounds and voices,
even unto me briefly describing it for sentient beings throughout immeasurable and boundless worlds.
The marvelous conduct of form, most supreme and vast, attains accomplishment.
At that time, the Tathāgata spoke these verses:
"Various battles are mastered in emptiness; Like planting a precious nature, it shines forth."
If a blue lotus blooms in a pond, its color is more radiant than that of a victorious hero;
that person is entirely transcendent and luminous, such that even the *Vijñāna-mantra* cannot equal him.
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed the Lord of Secrets, Vajrapāṇi.
Furthermore, he spoke in verse:
"To speak briefly of the common dharma: for those wise ones dwelling in the secret realm, first practice the preliminary rites, and then demonstrate the most excellent signs."
Regarding the regions, three types are taught:
the low-lying and damp, the dry, and those situated on high plateaus;
that which is inhabited by wise men is called an excellent land. Regarding the Middle Country, three types are taught.
The places for seeking accomplishment are all accessible to those of the three types of wisdom;
one should observe that they consist of both the pure and the impure, as well as the three kinds of celestial wonders. Within each of these, there are further distinctions.
Each is divided into three types: those known as the kings of rivers, lakes, oceans, and mountains are called the most excellent places of accomplishment;
those with both pure and impure qualities are called middling places of accomplishment;
and if it is a cemetery or a forest, [it is an inferior place].
This is called an impure place; this teaching concerns the three types of places for accomplishment in all locations.
One should not dwell in places where there are wicked kings, thieves, famine, or scarcity;
for the practitioner, such places present obstacles and difficulties.
One should not dwell on that ground; in this teaching, all [conditions] of extreme cold, heat, and rain are strictly prohibited.
One should recite during the three seasons in order to nurture one’s intention, and thus one should encompass these three times.
Again he addressed Vajrapāṇi: "Secret accomplishment cannot be found apart from this;
because accomplishment is attained within these scriptural teachings, they are called 'secret.
[This concludes] the distinctions regarding the homa hearth."
One should perform [rites] in secret; the three types [of rites], such as *śāntika* and so forth, should not be performed in one place.
If one performs *homa* in a single location, the *homa* hearth will inevitably be erroneous.
This applies if one uses the hearth for subjugation (*abhicāruka*).
One should not perform the rite of pacification (*śāntika*);
just as milk placed in a vessel containing poison will surely be ruined, one speaks of three types of hearths by carefully examining three matters. Other teachings also speak of three.
The hearth makes such distinctions; therefore, it is applied accordingly and thus there is no contradiction.
It is clearly permitted to use cow’s ghee for *kṣullaka-tṛṇāṅkura* (small grass sprouts), as well as for *udumbara* and celestial wood.
Furthermore, using milk-wood and saffron together, perform homa at the three times of day for the purpose of pacifying calamities;
one will thereby obtain various benefits. If one's medicinal substances have been stolen, [perform this rite].
One should employ black sesame mixed with honey for regular use;
likewise, one should employ white mustard seeds with the palāśa wood and devadāru wood for the homa, while offering praise.
Regarding these three kinds of substances, one should perform the *homa* oblation with clarified butter (*ghṛta*).
At that time, the Blessed One Śākyamuni again addressed the Lord of Secrets, Vajrapāṇi, saying:
In this context, for the sake of benefiting sentient beings,
the King of Teachings (Śāstrarāja) further speaks these verses:
These mantras and vidyās were spoken: the various great majestic powers of the cultivated Uṣṇīṣarāja;
the various mantras and vidyās of immeasurable and most marvelous power, including the Buddhalocanā and other vidyās.
I have previously proclaimed the accomplishment of all aims and benefits, as well as the mudrās and so forth;
for the sake of those seeking accomplishment, this Universal King of Mantras shall yield its fruit.
I shall now explain the mudrās for the sake of attaining siddhi;
though they are of one nature, I shall describe them in various ways.
First, I shall explain the general Buddha-uṣṇīṣa mudrā: interlace the fingers of both hands with the palms facing inward to form fists.
Join the two middle fingers together and bend their upper joints.
This is the general seal for all Buddha-uṣṇīṣas;
it can accomplish all aims and benefits.
By beholding this mudrā, one sees as if before one's eyes all the Buddhas;
the yakṣas who are difficult to subdue, the hosts of nāgas and asuras,
and all the rākṣasas— by the majestic power of this mudrā.
All were melted away, and they were struck with terror.
This is the Great Mantra, the Heart of All Buddha-Uṣṇīṣas: *Namaḥ samanta-buddhānāṃ oṃ taruṃ bandha svāhā*. He then spoke these verses:
If one obtains this mudrā, one will be able to attain all forms of peace and happiness;
for kings and others in the world, it will constantly bring benefit,
and those who seek the benefit of the Dharma will certainly obtain it.
If one obtains this mudrā, all sufferings will be completely extinguished;
by means of this fundamental mudrā of all Buddha-uṣṇīṣas,
one accomplishes all activities.
The practitioner who guards the sense faculties shall,
using this root seal,
move the tips of the middle fingers back and forth.
This is called the mudrā for invitation;
it is universally applicable to all as previously described,
using each respective mantra.
Use this root mudrā for all purposes.
Incense, flowers, burnt offerings, food and drink, lamps, and so forth— apply these with this mudrā.
Using the same mudrā as before,
with the tips of the two middle fingers joined like a ring—
this is the mudrā for welcoming the Fire Deity.
The mantras have already been explained as before.
When dismissing the fire deity,
one should pull the mudrā outward.
This immediately constitutes the fire-god dispatching mudrā.
Furthermore, this same mudrā, according to the previous procedure for the Buddha-uṣṇīṣa mudrā for accomplishing activities,
[is formed] with the tip of the right middle finger.
Bend the upper joint.
Press the upper joint of the left middle finger against the face.
This is the *Cūḍā-bhañjana-mudrā* (the Seal of Crushing the Crown).
One is able to perform extraordinary deeds and accomplish all tasks;
one should utilize this for protecting the body and establishing the boundary (sīmā).
Furthermore, shift the left middle finger so that its upper joint is bent and pressed down.
The upper phalanx of the right middle finger is the *Cūḍāmaṇi-mudrā* (Crest-Jewel Seal).
Its mantra has already been explained previously.
This is called the Destroyer of the Summit;
it is that which can subdue those who are difficult to subdue when great obstacles and difficulties arise.
With this, one should protect the body according to the general mudrā as previously described.
Bend the third joint of the right middle finger and rest it against the first joint of the left middle finger;
because this purifies the site, when seeking accomplishment, use this to destroy [obstacles] at the crown of the head and bind the protection of the site.
Shift the left finger as before. By means of this seal, protect the locations that are the heart-crests (*uṣṇīṣa*) of all Buddhas.
One should employ the crest-destroying seal for self-consecration; one should constantly use this seal.
If a person obtains this seal, they will be able to purify the recitation chamber;
at all times during their ablutions, the practitioner should employ it,
for by reciting this mantra, that person shall be free from all obstacles.
Employ them in their proper sequence; this mudrā of the *samaya* of one’s own family is to be used constantly.
For the practitioner of mantras, there shall be no demons within this teaching of the Buddha-uṣṇīṣa.
The Buddha spoke thus: "Regarding the aforementioned mudrā, place the two middle fingers upon the backs of the hands with their tips touching like a ring.
This is the Invincible Crown (Ajita-śekhara), which can extinguish all sins."
The mantra has already been taught; it can eliminate all evil dreams and accomplish auspicious matters.
One should employ this great mudrā when about to lie down to sleep, and if one constantly recites it oneself.
It can extinguish various obstacles; I have now explained it briefly.
A detailed exposition is immeasurable, but here I have given a summary for those who practice the Buddha-uṣṇīṣa together with the Buddhalocanā mantra.
Recite this to seek siddhi; within all assemblies, the cultivation of mantras is taught as liberation.
All Tathāgatas and Bodhisattvas thereby attain peace and happiness, obtain benefit and profit, and increase their diligence and great power.
Diligently practicing for the benefit of sentient beings, One completely eliminates all doubts and delusions.
Therefore, O Vajra Lord of Secrets, listen attentively As I proclaim it for you.
I have briefly explained this in accordance with the meaning; This is the secret practice for the wise.
Performing homa at the three times with celestial wood, sesame seeds, and ghee mixed with milk, one should recite this King of Joy Mantras.
Now I shall explain the accomplishment of the Lord of Mantras, as well as the practice of recitation and homa;
these three aspects are explained as mutually supporting one another.
Within each of these individual practices, the recitation and cultivation are explained as threefold:
body, speech, and mind, taught in their proper sequence. Furthermore, it should be known that for the sake of increasing accomplishments through such aspiration, three types are again taught:
those who roam in the heavens, those who travel through space, and those who dwell upon the earth.
There are three types of pursuits for their accomplishment:
seeking the fulfillment of desires, seeking wealth, and seeking the Dharma.
One should recite with diligence according to the specific *siddhi* sought, in order to attain all accomplishments.
One should properly construct a *caitya* according to the Dharma; for one who seeks accomplishment with right view and great compassion, that accomplishment will not be difficult.
In this present life, one shall obtain supreme peace and happiness, and in future lives, one will surely attain liberation. Many people of antiquity have attained accomplishment.
Through the cultivation of the Greatly Wondrous and Extraordinary King of Uṣṇīṣas— I myself have cultivated this King of Buddha-Uṣṇīṣas—
at that time, the Bhagavān Tathāgata Śākyamuni beheld immeasurable and boundless worlds with his Buddha-eye.
Again, he addressed Vajrapāṇi, speaking in verse:
"The vows and the rules of conduct, Both the means and the ends, Have already been explained among all the teachings; Now, within this very teaching..."
One should practice accordingly; by means of that noble Amṛtakuṇḍalī Vidyārāja,
one should constantly practice the ritual methods I have taught for the cultivation of the three families.
By the power of those mantras, all obstacles are completely removed;
as taught in the *Vidyārāja-sūtra*,
the mudrās of the Wrathful Kings and all their ritual procedures are entirely employed herein.
One should not eat onions, garlic, radishes, or leeks;
nor should one smear the body with oil,
nor consume any oily substances or impure foods, as prescribed by other teachings.
One should not eat anything; for the practitioner seeking *siddhi* always seeks a pure body,
one should therefore apply the *anavamṛtyu-mantra* to the five purities, doing so every half-month.
All other teachings that have been taught are practiced entirely within this;
I have explained them here in brief. What has not been explained at length here was explained in other sūtras by all the Tathāgatas.
The Dharma-nature of mantras was practiced and taught by all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas;
abiding in the form of those mantras,
they traverse the world, extensively performing all manner of beneficial purposes.
For the sake of those of inferior wisdom, I have fully described his majesty;
now I shall speak but a small portion, praising his virtues,
for even in a hundred eons one could not fully describe the Wheel-Turning King.
The nature of this wondrous and extraordinary Dharma— this merit is inexhaustible,
utterly inexhaustible, and unattainable. If one attains this King of Teachings,
that person is equal to the Tathāgata and likewise equal to the Bodhisattvas.
Having paid homage to the Celestial Sura, one’s mind attains non-retrogression and constantly gains such [realization].
All the provisions for awakening accumulated in previous lives are due entirely to the Lord of Secrets.
Possessing the power of great majesty and spiritual authority,
you should know that those sentient beings will always attain a pure body; if they obtain this King of Teachings,
they shall all attain everything and realize the state of the Honored One Among Two-Legged Beings.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra,
the Lord of Secrets Vajrapāṇi, the great bodhisattvas and other bhikṣus,
as well as all the world’s devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, and so forth, [were filled with joy].
Having heard what the Buddha had spoken, they rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
